reviews.text: Just like The Simpsons, this review series has been running too long. I LOVE The Simpsons. The show has really shaped humor and culture for hundreds and hundreds of people. The show’s peak was from seasons 2-8, from 1991 to 1997. So, dear reader, you might be asking along with me: why the hell did they wait until 2007, far past when people had been saying the show had been running too long, to make The Simpsons Movie? Who the hell knows, but it really is a detriment. While the think the film definitely has its very funny moments, it lacks a lot of the intelligence, both in the humor and emotion, that the show had. The film feels like a long version of a Simpsons episode, which really doesn’t work. I think that even if you’ve never written anything in your life, the structure of a 22 minute episode is far different from the structure of a 90 minute movie. I think a lot of movies based off shows have that issue, such as The South Park Movie, but that film worked much better for a few reasons. 1. The humor in The South Park Movie was consistently gutbustingly hilarious, whereas in The Simpsons Movies, while there aren’t any stinker jokes, the majority of them are just ok. There aren’t a lot of jokes I’ll be quoting over and over all watching it. 2. The South Park movie actually plays out like a film, the story is coherent, emotional beats pay off, running jokes resolve, and you feel like you actually watched something of cinematic scale. The Simpsons movie feels a lot looser, like a TV episode, but that means that plot lines don’t make sense, or don’t resolve, the emotional bits don’t really work out, and it overall feels less cinematic. 3. The South Park Movie did something above and beyond the show. The film had a massive scale, a lot of the animation was upped, and there were a bunch of over the top Broadway style musical numbers, stuff you wouldn’t see on a typical South Park episode. The Simpsons Movie feels like an episode of The Simpsons, even down to the animation. There is very little to distinguish the film from an episode. Homer’s opening joke of “why do we pay to watch something we get on TV for free” really feels indicative of the film’s quality. Overall, not really a bad film, but not really a must watch. Definitely only recommend it for hardcore fans.

Uma experiência cinematográfica muito inteligente e autoconsciente. Os Simpsons definitivamente já tiveram dias melhores, e isso não é nenhuma novidade, mas é impossível não sorrir ao ver esses personagens de volta às telonas. O roteiro começa muito bem, com uma premissa inteligente e várias ideias genuinamente engraçadas. O problema é que, em algum ponto perto da metade, parece que eles se esqueceram completamente da própria premissa e o filme começa a se perder. Mesmo assim, é difícil não se divertir. E talvez a falta de ambição seja justamente uma das coisas mais admiráveis sobre a série. Os Simpsons não precisam reinventar a roda. Continua sendo grosseira, ácida, estúpida e estranhamente cativante na medida certa. Realmente não precisamos de muito mais. Uma das melhores piadas acontece quando os religiosos percebem que o fim do mundo chegou e que não foram salvos. Em completo desespero, eles correm para o bar em busca de uma bebida, enquanto as pessoas que já estavam no bar correm para a igreja em busca de salvação. É uma inversão tão simples, absurda e brilhantemente cínica, o tipo de piada que eles fazem parecer fácil. Eu ri muito disso. Desde o primeiro fotograma, este é Os Simpsons em sua essência. Não há nenhuma tentativa de tornar a série maior, mais profunda ou mais importante do que realmente é. É simplesmente uma boa e velha visita a Springfield, agora em uma tela muito maior. Talvez não seja um retorno à era de ouro, nem de longe, mas depois de todos esses anos, passar algumas horas com esses velhos amigos ainda é melhor do que assistir a mais uma reprise.

Llevar una de las comedias más influyentes de la historia de la televisión a la gran pantalla era una maniobra inevitable, pero cargada de riesgos. Estrenada tras años de especulaciones y en un punto donde la serie de televisión ya mostraba signos claros de desgaste creativo, Los Simpson: La película asumió el reto de transformar una dinámica televisiva de 22 minutos en un evento cinematográfico de escala global. El resultado es un largometraje sumamente entretenido, vistoso y con picos cómicos altísimos, aunque empañado por decisiones narrativas que se alejan de la esencia más pura de Springfield. El apartado visual es, sin lugar a dudas, uno de sus puntos más sólidos. La transición hacia un dibujo más estilizado, apoyado por sombreados digitales y una paleta de colores vibrante, le otorgó al largometraje la escala de evento que exigía el cine. La dirección aprovecha las dimensiones de la pantalla grande para desplegar secuencias mucho más dinámicas —como la construcción de la cúpula sobre Springfield o el escape de la familia—, respaldadas por una banda sonora de John Powell que eleva la tensión sin perder la ironía característica de la franquicia. Sin embargo, el núcleo de la historia tropieza en la definición de sus prioridades. El conflicto central opta por apoyarse de forma casi exclusiva en una crisis matrimonial entre Homero y Marge, una fórmula narrativa ampliamente explotada en la serie que aquí se percibe cargada de clichés románticos. La decisión de volcar la carga emotiva en el reencuentro de la pareja le resta espacio al desarrollo de otras dinámicas de la ciudad y fuerza un todo sentimental que por momentos se siente ajeno a la acidez satírica que convirtió a la serie en un fenómeno cultural. A esto se suma una caracterización de Homero que no termina de asentarse. Si bien cuenta con momentos memorables dentro del metraje, se extrañan aquellos rasgos de su personalidad que construyeron sus mejores épocas en televisión: esa mezcla única entre tontería entrañable, momentos de astucia involuntaria y una relación más auténtica con sus vecinos y su entorno. En la película, gran parte de sus acciones quedan subordinadas a empujar el conflicto romántico, dejando en segundo plano su faceta como catalizador del caos social de Springfield. Los Simpson: La película funciona muy bien como pieza de entretenimiento rápido y cumple con el cometido de reunir a generaciones frente a la pantalla. Posee un ritmo ágil y chistes que han quedado grabados en la cultura popular, pero al balancear los elementos, queda la sensación de que prefirió ir a lo seguro antes que arriesgarse a construir un relato verdaderamente memorable. Un hito visual y nostálgico que aprueba con solvencia, pero que se queda lejos del brillo de los mejores años de la familia amarilla. Una entrega entretenida y técnicamente impecable que cumple con el espectáculo visual que exige la gran pantalla. Sin embargo, su dependencia de un conflicto romántico trillado y la pérdida de matices clave en Homero le impiden alcanzar el nivel de los mejores capítulos de la serie.

O mueres siendo la mejor comedia animada de la historia o vives lo suficiente para hacer una parodia de ti mismo. La película de los Simpson es bastante polarizante para mí. Salió en una época donde la serie ya estaba en declive y llevaba un par de años sin las voces originales en latino. Es inevitable compararla con los años dorados de la serie y ahí es cuando la película se siente sin esa gran carisma de las primeras 10 temporadas. Incluso en su fecha de estreno no me terminó de convencer, la comedia había perdido algo de chispa y las caracterizaciones de los personajes eran cada vez más planas. Homero en esta película es insufrible, cruel, extremadamente irresponsable y bobo. Lejos de ese padre torpe pero amoroso que solía ser. Tendrá su arco de redención al final, que al menos medio funciona. La serie se caracteriza por sus variadas estrellas invitadas y aquí me agrada la aparición de Green Day. La trama del domo y la destrucción de Springfield está ok. Los Simpson significan mucho para mí, marcaron mi infancia. Quisiera darle mejor calificación por mi amor a la serie, pero prefiero poner la temporada 6 en DVD que ver esta peli de nuevo.

Having premiered nearly forty years ago, The Simpsons is one of the longest last series airing on television.  However you may feel about its quality as it progresses, it is a testament to how popular it is that it has lasted as long as it has.  Of course, given said popularity, it was inevitable that movie starring the residents of Springfield would come to fruition.  When it comes to series being adapted to film, The Simpsons Movie is not among the worst of its kind and is entertaining.  However, it does come with a few of its own drawbacks. The Simpsons Movie goes for a grander plotline that is more fitting for a ninety minute feature than a half hour special.  This time, it is a series of careless accidents brought upon by Homer Simpson that brings great danger to Springfield.  Homer has been known for getting into trouble because of his stupidity or outright selfishness but it's a whole town that's at stake because of his flaws as opposed to matters with family or close friends.  It is a plot that does fit in with what the series was about, even having some clever political jokes here and there. Where the film does suffer a little is that, even with the more epic storyline, it also feels like an extended episode of the show.  This might hit a little differently for people who watch the show religiously while newcomers may be confused.  There are a few laughs to be found from fourth wall jokes and innuendos (some of which would have been censored on the actual show) but it also feels like it's fan service.  It's especially evident when random recurring characters pop up to do what the audience expects without really contributing too much to the actual plot.  Furthermore, the moments that are meant to feel emotional feel a little too quick to make way for some more jokes and action set pieces. The animation of the film keeps true to that of the show along with Matt Groening's own style.  It has been clearly been upgraded for a cinematic outing as it adds more shading and color, reflecting the higher budget.  At times it is even more fluid, partially a result of some former Disney animators having a hand in the making of it (There are a couple of humorous jokes at their expense as well).  It's a style that may not appeal to everyone, but fans of the show should be pleased that it doesn't go for something completely different on a technical level. All the original cast members return to voice their respective characters.  Dan Castellaneta does manage to capture Homer's dimwitted nature.  It is a little hard to get behind the character at times due to how emotionally distant he is for much of the film but Castellaneta is still having fun.  Julie Kavner gets more of a chance to show some range as Marge Simpson.  Bart feels a bit more short changed as he does have a potentially compelling plot but it's not given enough development though Nancy Cartwright still brings her A-game.  Albert Brooks is entertaining as a newcomer, the villainous Russ Cargill, who takes advantage of Homer's accidents in order to destroy Springfield. The Simpsons Movie is a mostly humorous, if slight adaptation of the series.  Much of the time it does feel like it is pandering to fans or stretching out a story way too thin.  Still, its entertainment value lies on its production, the voice acting and some clever writing and jokes.  It is one of the more decent theatrical adaptations of an animated TV show.

It's fine, as the potential finale to the show it's pretty good so the fact it went on for 20 more years(!) isn't a deduction in retrospect. It has the TV-to-movie problem of it being a comedy but requiring high stakes to justify its existence and the runtime. It is obviously a funny concept, and some jokes are a bit darker than the show (I'd forgotten they wanted to lynch Maggie - crazy they all moved past it) but the marriage crisis doesn't work for me in a Simpsons comedy. I think maybe because the soul-searching part never clicked with me, but also, it factually kills the vibe. It's a great character dynamic and is a high stake, but is that what we want from a comedy? Maybe it's just not a comedy style that works outside of a runtime crunch as they did in the golden age. Checking out the deleted scenes for the first time, there is a recency bias, but I wish they were left in. They feel like good writing and paid off some visual setups that didn't in the theatrical cut. You can see the sports stadium is cut in half by the dome, but only upon seeing the deleted scene we get the pay-off. First act is the highlight, the writing holds up and is still easily quotable. I find the Green Day stuff very boring, self-starring celebrity cameos are never interesting, and then it's a fairly gradual decline until the credits. It's barely a credit to an animated movie but it was nice to scan the crowd scenes and see some deep-cut Simpsons characters. We'll see how the new movie is. Hopefully it is truly the finale and Julie Kavner can finally rest her poor voice.

This was like nine year-old me’s favorite movie when it came out, and revisiting it nearly twenty years later, it’s hard to divorce the movie from my nostalgia. I still enjoyed it, but I definitely don’t find it as funny as I used to. I still laughed a couple of times throughout. I noticed weird sound mixing and animation errors here that aren’t big problems but confusing all the same. Why was Lard Lad white and not yellow? Why was that one Martin line towards the end muffled as fuck? What’s up with the drabber color palette towards the latter half, which doesn’t seem to be of thematic purpose? How the heck did The Simpsons afford the little Alaskan log cabin, was it really just $1000? Also, explaining the joke by changing Rainier Wolfcastle’s name to Schwarzenegger was lazy as fuck. The Bart skating naked sequence is still the highlight and full of great visual gags even if it’s the same joke throughout. There’s lots of fun visual gags in this movie overall.
